reagents.name: Zinc, pieces
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of zinc metal, as shot, sheet, foil or granules, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
On this bench a piece of zinc goes into copper(II) sulfate solution and another into dilute hydrochloric acid: pieces, not dust. The supplier's sheet for zinc as shot, sheet, foil and granules prints no signal word and no hazard statement, and puts the fire hazards with the dust. It keeps the metal from strong acids. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet for zinc shot says that zinc gives hydrogen with acids, as it does here on purpose: no flame is brought near that tube. It names dermatitis, and for the eyes asks 15 minutes or more of flushing with water and a doctor at once. A third's calls zinc very toxic to water life: it is kept out of drains and waterways.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Copper(II) sulfate solution, 1 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, the solid and pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H315+H319: Causes skin and serious eye irritation

note.value:
The solution on this bench is 1 mol/L copper(II) sulfate; the statements above are those of the solid it is made from. The same supplier's sheet for solutions of 0.5 M to 1.5 M gives Warning, with H302, harmful if swallowed, and H315 with H320, irritation of skin and eyes. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and for no eating or drinking near the solution.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: NOAA's record of the solid has the eyes flushed with water for 20 minutes to 30, with a hospital or a poison centre called meanwhile, and the skin flooded with water, then washed with soap. If any is swallowed, the solid's sheet has a poison centre or doctor called at once. It keeps the salt from magnesium and from finely powdered metals.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Magnesium, ribbon
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of magnesium metal, as turnings or ribbon, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
On this bench a short strip of magnesium ribbon is burned in a flame, and another goes into dilute hydrochloric acid. The supplier's sheet for the metal as turnings or ribbon keeps it from heat, sparks and flames, and from acids and water: here it meets a flame and an acid on purpose, as the experiments. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: by NOAA's record its flame is intensely white and very bright, with a dense white smoke. A magnesium fire is never put out with water, which the sheet says reacts violently with it, nor, by NOAA's record, with foam or carbon dioxide: dry sand or a class D extinguisher is used. With dilute acids it gives off hydrogen, a gas that burns.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Hydrochloric acid, 1 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of concentrated hydrochloric acid (6 M to 12 M), from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H314+H318: Causes severe skin and eye burns and damage
H332+H302: Harmful if swallowed or inhaled
H290: May be corrosive to metals

note.value:
The acid on this bench is 1 mol/L hydrochloric acid; the statements above are those of the concentrated acid it is made from. The same supplier's sheet for 0.1 M to 2.4 M keeps Danger and, under H314, says that it burns the skin severely and damages the eyes; under H335, that it may irritate the airways; under H303, that it may be harmful if swallowed.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet for weaker, 0.5 M acid asks more at the eyewash: eyes are flushed for 15 minutes or more and a doctor is seen at once. NOAA's record adds 15 minutes more where no doctor has come. The first sheet calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and a fume hood or a well-ventilated room; splashed clothing comes off at once.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Copper, pieces
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of copper metal, the solid and not its powder or dust, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
On this bench a piece of copper goes into dilute hydrochloric acid: a solid piece, not a powder. The supplier's sheet for copper prints no signal word and no hazard statement. It says that the metal in bulk does not burn, though its dust may, and keeps it from strong acids, nitric acid above all. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: NOAA's record of copper, from a federal guide to its dusts and mists, has skin that it touches washed promptly with soap and water, and the eyes washed at once with plenty of water, with medical attention immediately. It names sore eyes and nose and dermatitis as what the dust does: the dust is another matter.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Calcium chloride solution, 1 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid calcium chloride (anhydrous), the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The solution on this bench is 1 mol/L calcium chloride; the statements above are those of the solid it is made from. The same supplier's sheet for the solution, whose table of composition stops short of 15% of the hydrated salt (this strength is under that: 147 g in a litre, by this project's working), prints no signal word and no hazard statement. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet for a solution ten times weaker gives Warning and H320: it irritates the eyes. This solution is taken to do so at least as much. For the eyes that sheet asks rinsing with water for 15 minutes; NOAA's record of the solid asks 15 minutes or more, and an eye doctor.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Sodium carbonate solution, 1 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid sodium carbonate (anhydrous), the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H303: May be harmful if swallowed

note.value:
The solution on this bench is 1 mol/L sodium carbonate; the statements above are those of the solid it is made from. The same supplier's sheet for the solution, whose table of composition runs from 1% to 20% (this strength is 106 g in a litre, by this project's working), gives Warning and one statement, H316: mild irritation of the skin. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: the solution's sheet has no statement for the eyes, and the solid's has one, H319. The solution is handled as the solid: eyes are rinsed with water for several minutes and a doctor is seen if they stay sore; skin is washed with plenty of water. The solid is kept from acids: this bench's acid and this solution are not mixed.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Iron(III) chloride solution, 0.5 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid iron(III) chloride hexahydrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The solution on this bench is 0.5 mol/L iron(III) chloride; the statements above are the solid's. The same supplier has no sheet for this strength: its sheet for 0.1 M or less gives Warning, with H316 and H320, mild irritation of the skin and the eyes. Its two sheets for a solution call for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: its sheet for 1 M to 2.3 M, the next strength up: Warning, with H303, H316 and H319, possible harm if swallowed and serious irritation of the eyes. The eyes are to be rinsed with water for several minutes. Both sheets also ask for flushing with water at once, kept up for 15 minutes or more, without saying whether that is for the skin or for the eyes.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Hydrogen peroxide, 3%
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of hydrogen peroxide solution, 2% to 6%, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The liquid on this bench is 3% hydrogen peroxide in water, inside the 2% to 6% that the sheet above is for, so its statements apply as they stand: it irritates the skin and can do serious damage to the eyes. The sheet calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing. Eyes are rinsed with water for several minutes, and a doctor is seen if they stay sore; skin is washed with plenty of water.

The sheet keeps the solution from heat, strong bases, reducing agents and anything that burns or is easily oxidised, and has it stored in the dark in a vented container. Here a few drops of iron(III) chloride are added to it on purpose: the tube is left open, and is never stoppered. No second document was read for this strength.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

looks.before: A grey piece of metal lies beside the tube.
looks.after: A red-brown coating covers the metal.

looks.before: The liquid is clear and blue.
looks.after: The liquid is still clear, and a paler blue than it was.

notes.value: The red-brown coating is copper metal. Zinc took the place of copper in the dissolved copper(II) sulfate, and the copper came out as a solid on the zinc.
The blue belongs to the dissolved copper(II) sulfate, so it fades as that is used up. The zinc sulfate made in its place has no colour in water.
One element took the place of another in a compound: a single replacement. Zinc can push copper out because it is the more active of the two.

looks.before: A silvery strip of metal is held in tongs, beside the burner.
looks.after: The strip burns with a white light, too bright to look at.

looks.before: Only the strip is in the tongs.
looks.after: The strip is gone. A white powder is left where it was.

notes.value: Magnesium joined with oxygen from the air and made magnesium oxide, a white powder. Two things became one: a combination.
Burnt in air, magnesium also joins with the air's nitrogen, so the ash is a mixture: magnesium oxide with magnesium nitride in it. The equation here is for the oxide alone.

looks.before: A silvery strip of metal lies beside the tube.
looks.after: Bubbles stream off the metal, fast.

looks.before: A grey piece of metal lies beside the tube.
looks.after: Bubbles rise from the metal, slowly.

looks.before: A reddish piece of metal lies beside the tube.
looks.after: No bubbles. The metal looks as it did.

notes.value: The bubbles are hydrogen. Magnesium and zinc each took the place of the hydrogen in the acid, and each went into the liquid as its chloride: a single replacement, twice.
Copper did nothing. It stands below hydrogen in the order of the metals, and a metal below hydrogen does not push hydrogen out of an acid.
The higher a metal stands in that order, the faster it works on an acid. So the three run, most active first: magnesium, zinc, copper.

stations.title: Calcium chloride and sodium carbonate solutions

looks.before: The liquid is clear and colourless. Nothing solid is in it.
looks.after: A white solid has formed and clouds the liquid.

notes.value: The white solid is calcium carbonate, which does not dissolve in water. The sodium chloride made with it stays dissolved, so it is not seen.
The two compounds traded partners: calcium went with carbonate, and sodium with chloride. That is a double replacement.

looks.before: The liquid is clear and colourless. Nothing rises in it.
The tube feels no warmer than the room.
looks.after: The tube feels warmer than it did.

notes.value: The bubbles are oxygen. Hydrogen peroxide came apart into water and oxygen: one thing became two, a decomposition.
It does this by itself, but far too slowly to see. The iron(III) chloride speeds it up and is not used up: it is a catalyst, so it is not in the equation.
The tube warmed because this reaction gives out heat.

tubeMicrolitres.rationale: About 3 mL of liquid in a tube: enough to cover a piece of metal. The amount is this lab's own, chosen for the drawing; no result depends on it.

mixMicrolitres.rationale: About 2 mL of each of the two solutions that are mixed. The amount is this lab's own, chosen for the drawing; no result depends on it.

dropsMicrolitres.rationale: Five drops of about 0.05 mL each: the little iron(III) chloride that is added. The amount is this lab's own, chosen for the drawing; no result depends on it.
